newsitem.title: USA: Cyprus leaders agree on steps to curb risks - U.S..
newsitem.headline: Cyprus leaders agree on steps to curb risks - U.S..

text.p: Greek and Turkish Cypriot leaders have agreed in principle to implement measures to reduce the risk of incidents along the divided island's ceasefire line, the United States said on Monday.

After talks with a U.S. envoy, "both (Cypriot) President (Glafcos) Clerides and (Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf) Denktash agreed to give their full support to immediate implementation of the package of measures proposed by the United Nations," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.

He stressed that the Clinton administration considered the tentative agreement to be progress, but "full support means they said they're going to give their full support to it. It doesn't mean they've signed on the dotted line yet."

Burns said U.N. representatives in Cyprus this week would hold talks with Greek and Turkish Cypriot leaders on the confidence-building measures proposed by the United Nations. These include unmanning some positions along U.N.-patrolled ceasefire lines in Cyprus, unloading weapons and adopting a code of conduct "which makes clear that force can only be used in life-threatening situations," he said.

He said U.S. envoy Carey Cavanaugh, who met Clerides and Denktash on Monday, also discussed with them a U.S.-sponsored ban on Greek and Turkish military flights over Cyprus. Talks on this question will continue when Cavanaugh visits Athens on Tuesday and Wednesday and Ankara on Thursday.

Cavanaugh, director of the State Department's Southern European Affairs Department, was in the region trying to revive Cyprus peace talks after a new flare-up in tensions that began when Cyprus signed a contract with Russia to buy a controversial anti-aircraft missile system.

Turkey threatened military action last week to stop deployment of the S-300 system. The United States condemned Cyprus' plans to acquire the anti-missile system but blasted Turkey for threatening to use force against Cyprus and raising the prospects of war between Turkey and its NATO ally, Greece.

In Nicosia, Cavanaugh on Monday pronounced the crisis defused after Clerides assured him his government would not bring any part of a controversial anti-aircraft missile system to the divided island for at least 16 months.

Burns hailed this as an accomplishment, even though he said several times last week that the system would not be deployed for at least that long. He said Clerides was standing by his decision to purchase the system "but has pledged to Carey Cavanaugh today that he will not deploy any aspect of it or introduce any element of it -- not even import the parts into Cyprus -- for 16 months."

Burns said that should be reason for Turkey to end its recent aggressive rhetoric. "There's no need for the government of Turkey to exaggerate the importance of the events this week. They have a lot of time to work with the Cypriot government to defuse any kind of misunderstandings."
Burns, building on Secretary of State-designate Madeleine Albright's confirmation hearing last week, reiterated that Washington "will be active diplomatically in 1997 on Cyprus."

"I can't anticipate specifically what the components of any American programme will be except to say that we are willing to put a considerable amount of diplomatic resources into resolving this misunderstanding and, in fact, trying to make progress on the broader question of peace in Cyprus," he said.

Cyprus has been divided since 1974 when Turkey invaded the north of the island after a coup in Nicosia engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece. Denktash declared a Turkish Cypriot state in 1983 that only Ankara recognises.
Turkey has about 30,000 troops in the north of Cyprus. There are 11,500 Greek Cypriot national guardsmen in the south.
